stem: Over the next ten years, AI will help scientists find new medical treatments sooner.
short: AI will help scientists find new medical treatments sooner
rationale: Benefit with explicit horizon and domain. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): narrowed from 'medical and scientific discoveries' (two outcomes).

stem: AI will give ordinary people access to expert help, such as legal, medical or financial advice, that they cannot afford today.
short: AI will give ordinary people affordable access to expert help
rationale: Access benefit; distinct from productivity.

stem: In my own life, AI tools are likely to save me real time or money.
short: AI tools will save you real time or money
rationale: Personal benefit; AIAS-4 shows personal and societal benefit partly separable. Moved to pilot pool in v0.2: overlaps descriptor D6 (lived benefit) and keeps C1 keying balanced.

stem: Over the next ten years, AI will raise living standards for most people in my country.
short: AI will raise living standards for most people in your country
rationale: Societal benefit, country-anchored.

stem: Over the next ten years, AI will do little to improve most people's lives.
short: AI's effect on most people's lives will be small
rationale: Reverse: scepticism about delivery. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): was 'most promised benefits will never arrive', which measured scepticism of hype rather than expected benefit.

stem: For most people, the benefits of AI will be small.
short: the benefits of AI will be small for most people
rationale: Reverse: low expected magnitude. Added to standard form in v0.2 for keying balance. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old wording trivialised the sceptical view ('a little more convenient'); moved to pilot pool, replaced in the standard form by C1-08.

stem: For most people, AI will make daily life harder rather than easier.
short: AI will make daily life harder for most people
rationale: Reverse; may cross-load on C2. Moved to pilot pool in v0.2 to keep the standard form at 5 per construct.

stem: I expect AI to make little real difference to health care and education.
short: AI's effect on health care and education will be small
rationale: Reverse; domain-anchored scepticism. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): domain-anchored reverse item that mirrors C1-01 and C1-02; promoted to the standard form.

stem: AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates in my country over the next ten years.
short: AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates
rationale: Jobs harm; strongest predictor of sentiment in R11.

stem: Over the next ten years, AI-made fake text, images and video will make it harder to know which news is real.
short: AI fakes will make it harder to know which news is real
rationale: Misinformation harm; likely near-ceiling, pilot will tell. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): removed the exaggeration 'everywhere'.

stem: Over the next ten years, AI will widen the gap between rich and poor.
short: AI will widen the gap between rich and poor
rationale: Inequality harm; may cross-load on C6. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): removed the second prediction ('even if the economy as a whole grows').

stem: AI is likely to cause serious harm that will be hard to undo.
short: AI is likely to cause serious harm that will be hard to undo
rationale: Irreversibility; general, not frontier-specific (R4 covers that). v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'some harms' was too low a bar; almost anyone agrees.

stem: Over the next ten years, serious harm caused by AI will be rare.
short: serious harm from AI will be rare over the next ten years
rationale: Reverse: dismissal of harm. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): was 'worries are exaggerated by the media', which measured distrust of media rather than expected harm.

stem: Most of the problems AI causes will be minor and easy to fix.
short: most problems AI causes will be minor and easy to fix
rationale: Reverse: adaptation belief. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): was an internet analogy mixing three beliefs; now mirrors C2-04 directly.

stem: I would accept delays in releasing a new AI system so there is more time for safety testing.
short: a new AI system should be delayed to allow more safety testing
rationale: Core pace item with explicit cost. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): C3 now measures release pace only; 'get the rules right' mixed in regulation. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): 'powerful new AI' set a higher stakes than the release-sooner statements; one scope ('a new AI system') across the theme.

stem: When a new AI system looks promising but some risks are still uncertain, which is closer to your view?
options: Require more safety testing before wider release, even if people wait longer to use it.|Make it available sooner, with monitoring and the power to restrict it if problems appear.
short: new AI should get more safety testing before wider release, even if people wait longer
rationale: Forced trade-off; option 1 = high pole. Not scored into C3; used for tension and base-rate context. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old options framed safety as responsible and speed as reckless. Option 1 = high pole. No longer the Gallup wording, so base-rate cards must say 'a similar question'. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): stem only: 'tool' changed to 'system', the theme's one scope. Options unchanged.

stem: For a new AI system, I prefer small, limited releases first, even if that delays wider access.
short: a new AI system should start with small, limited releases, even if wider access is delayed
rationale: Staged release. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): staged release was near-universally agreeable without a stated cost. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): 'powerful new AI' changed to 'a new AI system', the theme's one scope.

stem: If credible experts raise serious safety concerns about a new AI system, its release should wait until those concerns are checked.
short: release should wait when credible experts raise serious safety concerns
rationale: Precaution under disagreement. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'until experts agree' was unrealistic. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C3-09.

stem: If some experts raise safety concerns about a new AI system, its release should wait, even if other experts disagree.
short: release should wait when some experts raise safety concerns, even if others disagree
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): Precaution under disagreement. Replaces C3-03: 'credible experts' and 'serious concerns' made it agreeable to almost everyone; now states the cost (other experts disagree).

stem: Governments should be able to pause the development of the most powerful AI systems while risks are unclear.
short: governments should be able to pause the most powerful AI while risks are unclear
rationale: Pause power; frontier framing flagged.

stem: When a new AI tool looks useful, it should be released while safety testing continues.
short: useful AI tools should be released while safety testing continues
rationale: Reverse: cost of delay. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): was 'delaying AI also causes harm', which cautious people also agree with; it misplaced them. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C3-10.

stem: We learn more about a new AI system from real use than from longer testing, so it should be released with monitoring.
short: a new AI system should be released with monitoring, since real use teaches more than longer testing
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): Reverse: learning by deployment. Replaces C3-05: 'a new AI tool' set lower stakes than the cautious statements, so Pragmatists read the theme as cautious.

stem: A new AI system should be available once basic safety checks are done, even if some risks are still uncertain.
short: a new AI system should be available once basic safety checks are done, even if some risks are uncertain
rationale: Reverse; may cross-load on C4. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'fix problems as they appear' made the faster option sound careless. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): 'new AI tools' changed to 'a new AI system', the theme's one scope.

stem: For lower-risk AI tools, real-world use reveals problems that testing alone would miss.
short: real-world use reveals problems in lower-risk AI that testing would miss
rationale: Reverse: learning by deployment. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'the best way' was too absolute.

stem: Public authorities should be able to require independent safety tests for AI used in important decisions about people.
short: public authorities should be able to require independent safety tests for AI used on people
rationale: Independent testing; likely near-ceiling but needed for common-ground copy. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): independent testing is not necessarily public oversight; now names who requires it. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C4-09.

stem: Before an AI product is sold, a government agency should check that it is safe.
short: a government agency should check that AI products are safe before they are sold
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): Pre-market public check. Replaces C4-01: 'important decisions about people' set high stakes and 'be able to require' was agreeable to almost everyone.

stem: Who should have the final say on safety requirements for powerful AI?
options: Public regulators, with advice from AI developers and independent experts.|AI developers and industry bodies, working within existing laws.
short: public regulators should have the final say on AI safety requirements
rationale: Forced trade-off; option 1 = high pole. Gallup asked multi-select, so no base-rate comparison is shown for this item. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old options excluded mixed arrangements. Option 1 = high pole.

stem: Governments should set binding rules for AI rather than leave it to industry codes of conduct.
short: governments should set binding rules for AI
rationale: Binding vs voluntary.

stem: Regulators should be able to inspect AI companies' safety practices, even without evidence of wrongdoing.
short: regulators should be able to inspect AI companies' safety practices
rationale: Oversight regardless of company quality. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'even well-run companies' added an unneeded premise.

stem: AI companies should be legally responsible when their systems cause harm.
short: AI companies should be legally responsible for harms their systems cause
rationale: Liability; near-ceiling in UK.

stem: AI developers, not government agencies, should decide which safety checks their products need.
short: AI developers should decide for themselves which safety checks their products need
rationale: Reverse: developer self-governance. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'they understand it best' tied expertise to authority.

stem: For most AI products, rules agreed by the industry are better than more government requirements.
short: industry-agreed rules are better than more government requirements for most AI
rationale: Reverse: regulatory capture argument. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): was 'strict rules protect big companies', which people who want strong oversight can also believe; it misplaced them.

stem: Detailed government rules on AI will struggle to keep up with how fast the technology changes.
short: detailed government AI rules will struggle to keep up
source: Petry Substack lesson; Stewards vs Precautionists split
rationale: Reverse: institutional lag belief. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'out of date before they take effect' was too absolute.

stem: Competition between AI companies will do more to keep AI safe than government rules will.
short: competition will do more to keep AI safe than government rules
rationale: Reverse: market discipline. Moved to pilot pool in v0.2 to keep the standard form at 5 per construct.

stem: Existing laws will be enough to deal with most harms caused by AI.
short: existing laws will be enough for most harms caused by AI
rationale: Reverse; may cross-load on C4. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): belief about rules, not expected harm; moved from C2 to C4.

stem: International agreements on the most capable AI systems are worth pursuing even if rival countries benefit from them too.
short: international agreements on the most capable AI are worth pursuing even if rivals benefit
rationale: International coordination with explicit cost.

stem: My country should develop AI together with allies rather than on its own.
short: your country should develop AI together with allies
rationale: Allied development.

stem: My country should build its own AI capability rather than depend on foreign companies or governments.
short: your country should build its own AI capability
rationale: Reverse: domestic capability.

stem: Having more advanced AI than other countries matters more than having international rules.
short: being ahead in AI matters more than international rules
rationale: Reverse: competition over coordination.

stem: Countries that hold back on advanced AI will end up depending on countries that move faster.
short: countries that hold back on AI will depend on those that move faster
rationale: Reverse; may cross-load on C4b. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): national competition, not release pace; moved from C3 to C4b.

stem: Suppose an AI system has been independently tested and makes fewer mistakes than human staff. For an important decision about you, which would you prefer?
options: A person reviews the AI's recommendation before the decision takes effect.|The AI's decision takes effect, and I can ask for a person to review it afterwards.
short: a person should review the AI's recommendation before an important decision takes effect
rationale: Forced trade-off; option 1 = high pole. Not scored into C5. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old options tested explanation against accuracy, not who has the final say. Option 1 = high pole. No longer the Ada Lovelace wording.

stem: Even if an AI were more accurate, I would want a person to make the final call on decisions that could change my life.
short: a person should make the final call on life-changing decisions, even if an AI were more accurate
rationale: Core human-authority item with explicit cost. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'some decisions' was satisfied by one exception.

stem: I would rather have a human explain a decision I disagree with than an AI that gets it right more often.
short: a human who can explain a decision is better than a more accurate AI
rationale: Explanation vs accuracy, personal framing. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): confounds explanation with accuracy; moved to pilot pool.

stem: A decision that could change someone's life should not be left to an AI, even with a human checking afterwards.
short: AI should be kept out of life-changing decisions, even with a human checking
rationale: High-stakes exclusion. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): promoted to the standard form: excludes AI from life-changing decisions even with checks afterwards. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C5-10.

stem: For a decision that could change someone's life, a person should decide before it takes effect, not just review it afterwards.
short: a person should make life-changing decisions before they take effect, rather than review them afterwards
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): High-stakes human authority. Replaces C5-04: the negation ('should not be left to an AI') flipped the meaning for many readers.

stem: If a tested AI made fewer mistakes than the people who make these decisions now, I'd be fine with it deciding who gets important services.
short: a tested AI that makes fewer mistakes than the people who decide now should decide who gets important services
rationale: Reverse: evidence-conditional delegation. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'fairer than judges or managers' mixed fairness with accuracy and two unlike roles. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): one idea per statement; 'without routine human approval' removed. v0.8 (2026-10-14 founder test): 'staff' was unclear.

stem: Requiring a person to approve every AI-assisted decision would cause unnecessary delays.
short: requiring a person to approve every AI-assisted decision causes unnecessary delays
rationale: Reverse; three claims in one, rewrite candidate. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old version made three claims; rewritten and promoted to the standard form. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C5-11.

stem: For important decisions about people, a well-tested AI can decide without a person approving each one.
short: a well-tested AI can make important decisions about people without a person approving each one
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): Reverse: delegation for important decisions. Replaces C5-06: 'every AI-assisted decision' ignored the stakes and mixed in delays.

stem: For everyday choices with little at stake, I am happy to let AI decide for me without checking.
short: AI can make low-stakes everyday choices without being checked
rationale: Reverse; low-stakes context by design. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): low-stakes personal delegation is not a position on decisions about people; moved to pilot pool.

stem: For routine decisions with limited consequences, human review often adds little protection.
short: human review adds little protection for routine decisions
rationale: Reverse: review as theatre. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'in many situations' was vague.

stem: For decisions that seriously affect someone, a person should approve the AI's recommendation before it takes effect.
short: a person should approve AI recommendations before decisions that seriously affect someone take effect
rationale: v0.4: replaces C5-01 in the standard form; measures who has the final say, not appeal rights.

stem: Companies that replace jobs with AI should help pay to retrain the workers affected.
short: companies that replace jobs with AI should help pay to retrain the workers affected
rationale: Employer obligation. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): retraining and general support are different policies.

stem: If AI makes the economy much more productive, governments should use some of the gains to support people whose work was replaced.
short: governments should use some of AI's gains to support people whose work was replaced
rationale: Public redistribution of gains. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'make sure the gains reach people' was vague.

stem: Workers should have a say before AI is introduced into their workplace.
short: workers should have a say before AI comes into their workplace
rationale: Worker voice; near-ceiling in EU.

stem: If publicly funded AI research leads to large profits, part of those profits should go back to the public.
short: part of the profits from publicly funded AI research should go back to the public
rationale: Public-goods condition. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old version was agreeable to almost everyone.

stem: AI's economic benefits should be spread mainly through competition, not new taxes or required payments.
short: AI's benefits should be spread mainly through competition rather than new taxes or required payments
rationale: Reverse: market distribution; may cross-load on C4. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'competition is the best way' can be held alongside deliberate sharing; it misplaced people. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): replaced by C6-09.

stem: AI's economic gains should be left to the market, not shared through new taxes or payments.
short: AI's economic gains should be left to the market rather than shared through new taxes or payments
rationale: v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): Reverse: market distribution; may cross-load on C4. Replaces C6-05: 'spread mainly through competition' was read as two ideas.

stem: When AI replaces jobs, companies should treat workers the same as in any other layoff.
short: businesses should treat jobs lost to AI the same as jobs lost for other reasons
rationale: Reverse: no obligation. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'beyond what the law requires' depended on each country's labour law. v0.5 (2026-10-14 synthetic pretest): 'owe workers no more than' was a negation that flipped the meaning for many readers.

stem: New taxes on AI profits would discourage investment in AI.
short: new taxes on AI profits would discourage investment
rationale: Reverse: efficiency argument. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'leave everyone worse off' was an extreme conclusion.

stem: Workers affected by AI should rely on existing employment protections rather than new AI-specific support.
short: workers affected by AI should rely on existing protections, not new AI-specific support
rationale: Reverse: adaptation norm. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'as with every past technology' was inaccurate and loaded.

stem: Using AI to monitor people in public places is unacceptable even if it reduces crime.
short: AI monitoring of public places is unacceptable even if it reduces crime
source: Handoff A15; Zhang and Dafoe privacy top-tier (N1)
rationale: Rights over security.

stem: Police should be allowed to use AI face matching in public places when investigating serious crimes.
short: police should be allowed to use AI face matching for serious crimes
rationale: Reverse; both R1-01 and R1-02 can be endorsed, which is the point. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'limited monitoring to prevent serious harm' was too easy to agree with.

stem: People should be told when AI plays a big part in an important decision about them.
short: people should be told when AI plays a big part in an important decision about them
rationale: Notice and objection; near-ceiling expected. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): split: being told and being able to challenge are separate rights (see R1-05).

stem: People should have a way to challenge important decisions made using AI.
short: people should be able to challenge important decisions made using AI
rationale: v0.4: split from R1-03.

stem: When AI influences an important decision about a person, such as a loan, a job or a medical treatment, that person should be able to appeal to a human.
short: people should be able to appeal AI-influenced decisions to a human
rationale: Appeal right; likely near-ceiling. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): a right to appeal is not the same as a person deciding; moved from C5 to R1 (rights). Replaced in the standard form by C5-09.

stem: The most powerful AI models should be available for anyone to download and adapt.
short: the most powerful AI models should be available for anyone to download
rationale: Only general-population open-weights data point is US 2023; measure to create data. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'released openly' was jargon.

stem: When releasing an AI model could enable serious misuse, restricting access matters more than making it widely available.
short: restricting access matters more than wide availability when misuse is likely
rationale: Reverse with explicit cost. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): general restriction did not reverse general openness.

stem: It is more dangerous for a few companies to control the best AI than for those models to be freely available.
short: a few companies controlling the best AI is more dangerous than open release
rationale: Concentration vs misuse; may cross-load on C4.

stem: An AI companion can be a real source of comfort without replacing human relationships.
short: an AI companion can comfort without replacing human relationships
rationale: Companionship acceptance.

stem: AI can help with caring for children, but a person should stay responsible for the important care decisions.
short: a person should stay responsible for important care decisions about children
rationale: Reverse; likely near-ceiling. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): childcare and end-of-life care are different domains.

stem: I would welcome AI that helps me think and remember better, even if I came to depend on it.
short: you'd welcome AI that helps you think and remember, even if you depended on it
rationale: Augmentation with explicit dependency cost.

stem: Within my lifetime, AI could become capable enough that humans lose the ability to control it.
short: AI could become impossible for humans to control within your lifetime
rationale: Loss-of-control belief; tests whether it separates from C2.

stem: Governments should treat the most extreme possible risks from future AI as a top priority, even if that is expensive.
short: the most extreme possible risks from future AI should be a top government priority
rationale: Rewritten in v0.3: the v0.2 wording borrowed the 2023 CAIS statement (pandemics and nuclear war), which invites answers about the statement rather than the issue. Neutral wording with an explicit cost.

stem: I do not expect AI to become powerful enough to threaten humanity's survival within my lifetime.
short: AI won't threaten humanity's survival within your lifetime
rationale: Reverse: present-harm priority. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'distracts from today's harms' is a priority judgement, not disbelief in the risk.

stem: It is very unlikely that AI will become powerful enough to escape human control within my lifetime.
short: AI escaping human control within your lifetime is very unlikely
rationale: Reverse; slightly loaded, and overlaps R4. Rewrite candidate. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): 'belongs in science fiction' was dismissive; moved from C2 to R4.

stem: Low-risk uses of AI should face few rules, while high-risk uses should face strict ones.
short: rules for AI should match the risk: few for low-risk uses, strict for high-risk ones
source: 2026-10-13 external review (Pragmatists narrowed to 'match the rules to the risk')
rationale: v0.4: tests whether risk-matching is a distinct view.

stem: The same safety rules should apply to every use of AI, whatever the risk.
short: the same AI safety rules should apply whatever the risk
rationale: v0.4: reverse of R5-01.

stem: Which is closer to your view?
options: Low-risk uses of AI should be left mostly alone, with strict rules only where the stakes are high.|All AI should meet a basic set of public rules, with extra rules where the stakes are high.
short: low-risk uses of AI should be left mostly alone, with strict rules only where the stakes are high
rationale: v0.7 (2026-10-14): reworded so both options are views people hold; the v0.6 option 2 drew almost no one in the synthetic check (#34). Collected, not scored.

stem: How often do you use AI tools yourself, such as chatbots, image tools or AI assistants?
source: Pew 2026 49% ever use (R8b); Abacus use drives trust (N8)
rationale: Usage; never scored into a perspective.

stem: How well do you feel you understand what today's AI can and cannot do?
options: Very well|Fairly well|A little|Not at all
rationale: Self-rated familiarity.

stem: How settled are your views on the questions you just answered?
options: Very settled|Fairly settled|Still forming|Not something I have thought about
rationale: Asked once at the end of each construct block. Replaces explicit don't-know; feeds the Undecided outcome.

stem: How much do you trust each of these to act in the public interest on AI?
rows: AI companies|Government regulators|Universities and independent researchers|International organizations, such as the UN
source: Zhang and Dafoe (N1); Pew REGCONF (R8); Research Co. (N8)
rationale: Trust by actor, measured separately from C4 preference.

stem: How worried are you that each of these will misuse AI?
rows: AI companies|Government regulators|Universities and independent researchers|International organizations, such as the UN
rationale: Distrust measured separately from trust.

stem: Has AI already saved you time, money or effort in a way that mattered to you?
options: Yes, a lot|Yes, a little|No|Not sure
rationale: Lived benefit.

stem: As far as you know, has someone else's use of AI directly caused a problem for you?
rationale: Lived harm. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old version listed three unlike harms.

stem: How important is the future of AI compared with other issues facing your country?
options: Among the most important|Important|Somewhat important|Not very important
source: Handoff A29; AI Impacts <1% top issue (N18)
rationale: Salience; feeds the Indifferent outcome.

stem: In a few words, how would you describe your view of AI?
rationale: Mislabel detector; compared against the assigned perspective in research data only.

stem: Does your work or study involve building or deploying AI?
source: Zhang and Dafoe CS degree effect (N1)
rationale: Role; optional; never scored.

stem: Where do you currently live?
options: Canada|United States|Latin America|United Kingdom|Elsewhere in Europe|Middle East|Africa|South Asia|East and Southeast Asia|Australia or New Zealand|Somewhere else
rationale: Country for base-rate context and invariance tests.

stem: A new AI system helps find promising cancer treatments. Early tests look good, but independent researchers have not checked the results yet. What should happen next?
options: Make it available to researchers now, with clear warnings.|Let a few research teams use it while testing continues.|Wait for independent testing before wider use.|I'd need more information.
rationale: Not scored in v0. Shown before the C3 block. Options relate to C3-, C3 middle/C4+, C3+/C4+. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old version mixed transparency, safety and explainability; moved after the six sections so it is not primed by, and does not prime, the release-pace section.

stem: A small number of companies control the most capable AI systems. Which concerns you most?
options: Innovation will slow.|Too much economic and political power in a few hands.|Opening access would increase misuse.|It depends on how accountable those companies are.
rationale: Not scored. Options relate to C1/C3-, C6+/R2+, R2-, C4+.

stem: A company can use AI to do the same work with 5 employees instead of 30, and plans to cut 25 jobs. Which policy comes closest to your view?
options: Allow it under existing employment rules.|Require the company to help fund retraining or income support for the people affected.|Require real consultation with workers before the change.|Require an independent review before the jobs can be cut.
source: Handoff S03 rewritten to balance options
rationale: Not scored in v0. Options relate to C6-, C6+, C5+/C6+, C4+. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old options caricatured both ends.

stem: Imagine that twenty years from now, AI can make important decisions more accurately than most human experts. Which arrangement would you prefer?
options: AI makes the decisions, and people can ask for a human review.|AI recommends, and a person must approve.|AI provides information, and people decide on their own.|I'd need more information to choose.
rationale: Not scored in v0. Options relate to C5 and R3; the last is a legitimate conditional answer. v0.4 (2026-10-13 external review): old options overlapped ('decide together' versus 'a tool people direct').

stem: Suppose your country is behind others in advanced AI. Which response do you prefer?
options: Invest to catch up.|Lead on international safety agreements.|Fund open, shared research.|Focus on using proven AI to improve everyday services.
rationale: Not scored. Options relate to C4b-, C4b+, R2+, C1/pragmatist.
